case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, based on the complaint’s particular factual allegations, a generic-drug manufacturer can be plausibly alleged (at the motion-to-dismiss stage) to have “actively induced” infringement of a brand manufacturer’s method-of-use patents through its labeling and related conduct, despite a carved-out/limited indication under the Hatch–Waxman framework.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) (active inducement of patent infringement) (in the Hatch–Waxman/ANDA “skinny label” context for method-of-use patents).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Hikma and related entities) argue that the Federal Circuit applied an overly permissive inducement pleading/causation standard that effectively undermines Hatch–Waxman’s allowance for ANDA approval with a “skinny label” (carving out patented uses). They contend that truthful, FDA-required (or FDA-authorized) generic labeling for non-patented uses—combined with ordinary market realities like automatic generic substitution—should not, without more concrete allegations of purposeful encouragement directed to the patented use, suffice to plead the specific intent and affirmative acts required for inducement under § 271(b). Petitioners and supporting amici (including the United States, AAM, Henry Waxman, and scholars) emphasize that weakening the inducement standard will chill generic launches, raise drug costs (including for federal programs), and allow method-of-use patent holders to extend exclusivity beyond the statutory balance Congress struck.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Amarin and related entities) argue that, taking the complaint’s allegations as true and viewing the pleaded facts as a whole, Hikma plausibly engaged in affirmative conduct showing intent to cause physicians/pharmacists to use the generic in the patented manner. On their theory, even with a carved-out label, the ‘constellation of facts’—including how the generic’s materials were allegedly presented and understood in the marketplace—supports a reasonable inference that Hikma did more than merely sell an approved generic; it encouraged or facilitated substitution and use in the patented indication, satisfying § 271(b) at the pleading stage. Respondents also resist a rule that would require plaintiffs to negate every non-infringing explanation (e.g., investor “puffery”) at Rule 12(b)(6), asserting that plausibility can be met without conclusively ruling out lawful motives before discovery.
key_precedents: Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. (inducement requires knowledge and intent; willful blindness)
Twombly/Iqbal pleading framework (plausibility at Rule 12(b)(6), including competing inferences)
Hatch–Waxman Act/ANDA “skinny label” line of cases in the Federal Circuit (inducement via labeling/marketing in method-of-use contexts)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that a generic can “intend” infringement by launching into a market where automatic substitution predictably channels use to the patented indication—still falls short of § 271(b)’s requirement that the defendant “actively” induce infringement, which under Global-Tech means purposeful, use-directed encouragement. As Justice Thomas stresses, treating foreseeable downstream substitution dynamics and FDA-compliant skinny labeling as the inducing act risks untethering inducement from affirmative conduct and effectively penalizing the very § viii pathway Congress created. And as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Twombly/Iqbal require allegations that make culpable intent more than equally plausible; here the pleaded facts remain at least as consistent with lawful carve-out marketing as with a deliberate plan to cause infringing use. A narrow, pleadings-stage holding—leaving room for cases with concrete, patented-use-directed promotion or instructions—best preserves statutory coherence and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that, in practice, a skinny label plus predictable automatic substitution functions as an instruction for the patented use, but § 271(b)’s text requires that the defendant “actively” induce—i.e., take affirmative, use-directed steps to bring about infringement, not merely sell a lawful product in a market where infringement is foreseeable. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Global-Tech correctly ties inducement to knowledge plus a deliberate aim to cause infringement; that intent cannot be inferred solely from downstream substitution dynamics that Congress contemplated when it created the § viii carve-out pathway. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on the lawful baseline set by Hatch–Waxman reinforces that treating FDA-compliant carve-out labeling as the inducing act would effectively expand § 271(b) beyond its ordinary meaning and convert § viii compliance into a liability trap. Under Twombly/Iqbal, allegations equally consistent with lawful skinny-label marketing do not plausibly plead the specific, affirmative encouragement the statute requires at the motion-to-dismiss stage.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that Hikma could foresee—and perhaps even expect—that automatic substitution would channel sales into the patented use, but foreseeability is not what § 271(b) says: it requires that the defendant “actively induces,” i.e., takes purposeful, use-directed steps to bring about infringement. Chief Justice Roberts is right that under Global-Tech the intent inference must be tied to affirmative encouragement, and at the pleading stage Twombly/Iqbal do not permit liability where the alleged facts are at least as consistent with lawful § viii skinny-label compliance as with a scheme to promote the patented method. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Warner-Lambert underscores that truthful, FDA-authorized labeling for nonpatented indications ordinarily is not enough absent concrete promotional or instructional conduct aimed at the patented use. Treating predictable substitution dynamics as “active inducement” would, as a practical matter, convert Congress’s carve-out pathway into a liability trap and dilute the statutory term “actively.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the real-world claim that automatic substitution and predictable prescribing practices make a skinny-label launch functionally causative of infringing use, but foreseeability is not the same as § 271(b)’s requirement that a defendant “actively” and purposefully encourage the patented method. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Global-Tech’s specific-intent requirement and Twombly/Iqbal’s plausibility threshold persuades me that, where the pleaded facts are equally consistent with Congress-authorized § viii carve-out compliance, we cannot treat lawful labeling and ordinary market participation as the affirmative encouragement itself. Chief Justice Roberts’s workability concern also matters for access to medicines: letting generalized inferences from substitution dynamics and ambiguous corporate statements unlock discovery would chill generics and distort Hatch–Waxman’s balance, especially to the detriment of patients who rely on lower-cost drugs. I would still leave room for inducement where there are concrete, use-directed promotional or instructional acts aimed at the patented indication, but this complaint does not plausibly allege that.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that a skinny label can still operate as a de facto instruction when the generic knows substitution will predictably channel use toward the patented method. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 271(b)’s text—“actively induces”—and Global-Tech require purposeful, use-directed encouragement, not an intent inference built largely from foreseeable market mechanics that are equally consistent with Congress’s § viii carve-out pathway. Twombly/Iqbal matters here because the pleaded facts (FDA-compliant carve-out labeling plus ordinary sales) do not make the illicit-purpose inference more plausible than the lawful explanation; allowing discovery on that basis would risk turning § viii into a liability trap and upsetting statutory coherence. I would leave room for inducement where there are concrete allegations of patented-use-directed promotion or instructions, but this complaint does not plausibly plead that.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest respondent theory—that a generic “intends” infringement by exploiting automatic substitution and leaving label “breadcrumbs”—still collapses § 271(b)’s textual requirement of “actively induces” into mere foreseeability from lawful, Congress-authorized § viii conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, Global-Tech requires purposeful, use-directed encouragement, and on these pleadings Twombly/Iqbal do not allow an inference of specific intent where the alleged facts are at least as consistent with lawful skinny-label compliance as with inducement. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on the adverb “actively” is dispositive for me: absent concrete allegations of patented-use-directed promotion or instruction, we would be expanding inducement beyond its ordinary meaning and effectively turning Hatch–Waxman’s carve-out into a liability trap without clear statutory warrant. Our holding can remain narrow—dismissal on these allegations—while preserving liability where plaintiffs plausibly plead affirmative, targeted encouragement toward the patented method.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument is that, in the Hatch–Waxman ecosystem, a generic’s knowledge of automatic substitution plus awareness of the patented use makes intent to induce plausibly inferable, even with a § viii skinny label. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Global-Tech requires specific intent and “active” steps directed to bringing about infringement, and Twombly/Iqbal do not allow an inference of illicit purpose where the pleaded facts are at least as consistent with lawful, Congress-authorized carve-out marketing and regulatory compliance. Justice Thomas’s textual point about the adverb “actively” reinforces that foreseeability from ordinary market mechanics cannot substitute for affirmative encouragement (e.g., patented-use-directed instructions or promotion) at the pleading stage. Institutionally and practically, adopting respondent’s theory here would risk converting § viii into a de facto inducement trap and invite burdensome discovery on thin, equally lawful pleadings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best case is that, in a skinny-label market, a generic’s knowledge of likely off-label prescribing plus automatic substitution makes infringement so predictable that intent should be inferred. But as Justice Thomas underscores, § 271(b)’s text—“actively induces”—demands affirmative, use-directed encouragement, and Global-Tech’s framework does not allow us to replace purposeful promotion with mere foreseeability from lawful sales and FDA-compliant labeling. Chief Justice Roberts’s Twombly/Iqbal point is decisive at the pleading stage: where the alleged facts are at least as consistent with Congress-authorized § viii carve-out competition as with a deliberate scheme to cause the patented method’s use, the complaint has not plausibly alleged specific intent. I therefore do not see a precedent-based or textual basis to treat regulatory compliance and market mechanics as the inducing act itself, and I would reverse on the pleadings as framed here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that predictable automatic substitution makes infringing use foreseeable, so intent can be inferred from real-world consequences. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Global-Tech and § 271(b)’s requirement of “active” inducement demand purposeful, use-directed encouragement, and Twombly/Iqbal require factual allegations that make that culpable inference more plausible than the lawful explanation of FDA-compliant § viii skinny-label marketing. Justice Thomas’s textual emphasis on “actively” reinforces that we should not treat Congress-authorized carve-out compliance plus market mechanics as the affirmative act itself. On these pleadings, allowing discovery would risk converting the Hatch–Waxman pathway into a liability trap without concrete allegations of patented-use-directed promotion or instructions, so I remain for reversal.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only for “active inducement,” requiring affirmative acts and a purpose to bring about the infringing use, not merely conduct that foreseeably coincides with infringement. Global-Tech confirms that inducement turns on knowledge and specific intent, and Twombly/Iqbal require that the complaint plausibly support that culpable inference rather than rest on market “automatic substitution” dynamics and FDA-authorized, truthfully limited labeling under Hatch–Waxman’s § viii carve-out framework. On these allegations, the more plausible inference is lawful marketing of an approved non-patented indication, and allowing such “passive inducement” theories to proceed would risk undermining Congress’s balance for skinny-label generics and invite broad discovery on thin pleadings. A narrow reversal reinstating dismissal on these pleadings best preserves precedent on intent, respects the statutory scheme, and avoids destabilizing generic competition through an expanded inducement theory.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces infringement,” and the text—especially the adverb “actively”—requires affirmative steps undertaken with the specific intent to bring about infringement, not merely foreseeable downstream misuse of a lawfully sold product. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. makes clear that inducement demands both knowledge and purposeful conduct directed to the infringing use; allegations resting primarily on FDA-authorized “skinny label” content and ordinary substitution dynamics do not plausibly plead the requisite intent and affirmative encouragement. At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage under Twombly/Iqbal, a complaint must plausibly support an inference of inducement rather than lawful conduct consistent with Hatch–Waxman’s carve-out scheme, and generic compliance with FDA labeling for nonpatented indications is not, without more, “active” inducement. The Federal Circuit’s more permissive approach effectively expands § 271(b) beyond its text and threatens the statutory balance Congress struck in permitting ANDA approval with carved-out indications.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who "actively induces" infringement, which this Court has construed to require both knowledge and a purpose to bring about infringement through affirmative acts, not mere foreseeability or market dynamics. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. makes clear that inducement turns on specific intent (or at least willful blindness to infringement), and truthful, FDA-authorized skinny-label labeling for nonpatented uses—coupled with automatic substitution laws—does not, without more, plausibly allege purposeful encouragement of the patented use at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage under Twombly/Iqbal. Allowing a complaint to proceed on allegations that third parties “could infer” an infringing instruction from objectively non-infringing labeling would dilute the statutory term "actively" and undermine Hatch–Waxman’s Section viii carve-out framework by converting lawful generic marketing into inducement liability. Practical consequences reinforce that reading: a permissive inducement pleading standard in the skinny-label context would predictably chill generic entry and disrupt the balance Congress struck between method-of-use patents and generic competition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces infringement,” which under Global-Tech requires specific intent (knowledge that the induced acts constitute infringement) and affirmative conduct beyond the mere sale of a lawful product. Under Twombly/Iqbal, a complaint must plead facts making inducement plausible, not merely possible, and where the defendant’s conduct is facially consistent with lawful Section viii “skinny label” marketing, generalized allegations relying on automatic substitution or investor-facing “puffery” do not plausibly support the requisite intent without more concrete, use-directed encouragement. Preserving Hatch–Waxman’s balance and access to affordable medicines counsels against allowing inducement claims to proceed on thin inferences that would effectively nullify the statutory carve-out and invite costly discovery that chills generic entry. On these allegations, the better reading is that Hikma’s FDA-authorized limited labeling and ordinary market dynamics are inadequate, standing alone, to plausibly plead active inducement at Rule 12(b)(6).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires “active inducement,” meaning affirmative steps taken with the specific intent to bring about infringement, not merely lawful conduct that foreseeably results in some infringing uses. Under Global-Tech, knowledge and intent are essential, and at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage Twombly/Iqbal requires facts making the illicit-intent inference more than consistent with lawful explanations; a skinny label pursued under Hatch–Waxman’s § viii pathway is Congress-authorized baseline conduct that cannot itself plausibly supply the needed culpable encouragement. Federal Circuit skinny-label cases (e.g., Warner-Lambert v. Apotex) reflect that truthful, FDA-authorized labeling for non-patented indications—plus market realities like substitution—does not, without concrete allegations of targeted promotional or instructional acts tied to the patented method, constitute the “affirmative act” and specific intent § 271(b) demands. Because the complaint here is plausibly explained by lawful regulatory compliance and ordinary substitution rather than purposeful encouragement of the patented use, it should be dismissed (or at least narrowed) absent more specific inducement allegations.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only where a defendant "actively" induces infringement—an intent requirement this Court has treated as demanding knowledge and purposeful encouragement, not mere foreseeability. See Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A.; and under Twombly/Iqbal, a complaint must plead facts making that specific intent plausible rather than relying on conclusory assertions layered atop otherwise lawful conduct. In the Hatch–Waxman skinny-label setting, FDA-authorized labeling for nonpatented indications and ordinary substitution practices are lawful and expected; absent well-pleaded “other factors” plausibly showing a purpose to bring about the patented use, the inference of inducement is too speculative at Rule 12(b)(6). Allowing inducement to be pleaded on these facts would effectively convert Congress’s carve-out mechanism into a trap for generic entrants, stretching § 271(b)’s text beyond its ordinary meaning and upsetting the statutory balance without clear congressional command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Twombly and Iqbal require factual allegations that make liability plausible, not merely possible; where the alleged “inducing” conduct is largely the lawful, FDA-authorized skinny-label pathway Congress permitted under Hatch–Waxman, allegations equally consistent with legitimate generic competition do not plausibly show culpable intent. Section 271(b) and Global-Tech require affirmative acts undertaken with the specific intent to encourage infringement, not intent inferred primarily from automatic substitution and truthful labeling for non-patented indications. Absent particularized allegations tying specific statements or promotional conduct to the patented method-of-use and a plausible causal pathway to that infringing use, imposing inducement liability risks upsetting the statutory balance and chilling generic entry. Consistent with judicial restraint and workability, I would reverse and require more concrete, targeted facts before permitting discovery on inducement in the skinny-label context.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces” infringement, and that text—reinforced by Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754 (2011)—requires plausible allegations of knowledge of the patent and a purpose to bring about the infringing use, not merely foreseeability that infringement might occur. In the Hatch–Waxman “skinny label” setting, a complaint that rests chiefly on FDA-authorized labeling for nonpatented indications plus market realities like automatic substitution alleges, at most, lawful product distribution conduct rather than the kind of affirmative, culpable encouragement (e.g., advertising or instructions to practice the patented method) that § 271(b) targets. Applying Twombly/Iqbal, where the pleaded facts are equally consistent with lawful intent (e.g., compliance with FDA requirements, investor communications, ordinary sales) as with specific intent to induce the patented use, the inference of inducement is not “plausible” at Rule 12(b)(6). Holding otherwise would effectively convert Congress’s skinny-label pathway into a presumptive inducement trap, a result difficult to square with § 271(b)’s text and this Court’s insistence on purposeful conduct.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Twombly/Iqbal require factual allegations that make liability under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) a reasonable inference, not allegations that are merely consistent with infringement where a lawful explanation is at least as likely. Under Global-Tech, inducement demands specific intent and affirmative acts to bring about infringement; in the Hatch–Waxman “skinny label” setting, a complaint that principally relies on FDA-authorized labeling for non-patented uses plus predictable state-law substitution practices does not, without more targeted encouragement toward the patented use, plausibly plead the requisite intent. Given Congress’s designed balance permitting carve-outs, an overly permissive inducement-pleading rule would predictably chill generic entry and raise drug costs without a procedurally fair basis for forcing discovery on thin allegations. Accordingly, I would reverse and require more concrete allegations of purposeful, patented-use-directed encouragement to plausibly state an inducement claim.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, based on the specific complaint allegations, a generic drug manufacturer can be plausibly (at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage) alleged to have “actively induced” infringement of a brand’s method-of-use patents when the generic’s label carves out the patented indication but the generic’s other communications and market realities allegedly steer use toward the patented method.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) (induced patent infringement) (in the Hatch-Waxman context involving method-of-use patents and “skinny labels”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Hikma and related entities) argue that the Federal Circuit allowed an inducement claim to proceed on an overly expansive and speculative theory that effectively penalizes lawful “skinny label” marketing and ordinary, non-instructive communications (e.g., FDA-mandated labeling/approvals, truthful public statements, or routine commercial conduct) even when the patented indication is carved out of the generic label. They contend that inducement requires concrete, affirmative acts encouraging the patented use and a plausible showing of specific intent to bring about infringement—not merely knowledge that some infringement may occur due to substitution laws, physician practice patterns, or the therapeutic equivalence regime. Petitioners and supporting amici (including the United States, AAM, and Rep. Waxman) stress that relaxing the inducement/intent and pleading standards would undermine the Hatch-Waxman framework, deter generic entry, and raise drug costs, because brands could convert method patents into de facto barriers even where the generic complies with carve-outs and does not promote the patented use.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Amarin and related entities) argue that, on the “particular constellation of facts” pleaded, the complaint plausibly alleges active inducement: despite a carved-out label, petitioners allegedly engaged in affirmative conduct that predictably and intentionally caused physicians/pharmacists to use or dispense the generic in the patented manner. Respondents emphasize that inducement can be inferred from circumstantial evidence, including marketing context, public or investor-facing statements, and how the product is positioned in the market; they maintain the Federal Circuit correctly applied the plausibility standard by concluding the alleged conduct goes beyond mere knowledge of possible infringement and constitutes purposeful encouragement or facilitation of the patented use. They also resist a rule that would treat a skinny label as categorically dispositive against inducement at the pleading stage, arguing that such a rule would invite gamesmanship and allow generic makers to induce infringement through non-label channels.
key_precedents: Twombly/Iqbal pleading standard (referenced in oral argument via the idea that plaintiffs must plausibly rule out lawful explanations at the motion-to-dismiss stage)
Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. (inducement requires knowledge/intent; often central to § 271(b) intent analysis)
MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd. (inducement-by-promotion concept; frequently invoked by analogy in § 271(b) cases)

Federal Circuit skinny-label inducement line of cases (commonly including decisions like Warner-Lambert v. Apotex; AstraZeneca v. Apotex; GlaxoSmithKline v. Teva; although the provided excerpts do not enumerate them explicitly, they are the typical backbone of the dispute)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that, in Hatch-Waxman markets, a generic can anticipate—and may even economically benefit from—state substitution and AB-rating driving some patented-use prescribing, so intent should be inferable despite a § viii skinny label. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress, Global-Tech and Grokster require well-pleaded facts showing purposeful, affirmative encouragement of the patented method, not allegations that amount to foreseeable downstream infringement in a congressionally authorized regulatory pathway. Under Twombly/Iqbal, conduct equally consistent with lawful § viii compliance and ordinary commercial communications cannot alone plausibly establish the specific intent element of § 271(b); we can resolve this case narrowly by holding only that these pleadings—resting chiefly on “market realities” and generalized statements untethered to instructing the carved-out use—are insufficient. That minimalist approach preserves the possibility that different, more targeted promotional allegations could state an inducement claim, while preventing foreseeability from swallowing “actively induces.”

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s best point is that therapeutic equivalence and state substitution make some infringing uses highly predictable, so a launch plus public statements could imply intent—but that reduces § 271(b)’s text (“actively induces”) to mere foreseeability, contrary to its original public meaning requiring affirmative, purposive encouragement. Justice Gorsuch’s focus on “actively” is decisive under a textualist reading: Congress chose a verb connoting conduct aimed at producing a result, not simply selling a lawful product into a regulated market. Chief Justice Roberts is also right that Twombly/Iqbal bars inferring specific intent from allegations equally consistent with Congress’s authorized § viii carve-out and routine, non-instructive communications. Global-Tech and Grokster reinforce that inducement turns on purposeful, culpable steps directed to the infringing method; the pleadings described do not plausibly allege that kind of targeted encouragement for the carved-out indication.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains that, in the Hatch-Waxman ecosystem, AB-rating plus substitution laws makes some infringing use highly predictable; but predictability is not the same as the “purposeful, culpable” encouragement Grokster and Global-Tech demand, and reading it that way would drain “actively induces” of its textual force. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on Twombly/Iqbal is decisive for me: when the pleaded facts are at least equally consistent with lawful § viii compliance and routine commercial communications, the complaint has not plausibly alleged specific intent directed to the patented method. Justice Kagan’s “middle ground” is right in principle—skinny labels aren’t categorically dispositive—but it still requires concrete allegations of targeted promotion or instruction for the carved-out use, which this pleading (as described) does not supply. Given the practical consequences, collapsing intent into market foreseeability would convert Congress’s carve-out pathway into a liability trap and destabilize Hatch-Waxman’s operation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that Hatch-Waxman “market realities” (AB-rating, substitution laws, prescribing patterns) make some patented-use prescribing predictable, but predictability is not the same thing as the “purposeful, culpable” encouragement Grokster and Global-Tech require for § 271(b). Chief Justice Roberts’s Twombly/Iqbal framing is persuasive: when the pleaded facts are at least as consistent with lawful § viii skinny-label compliance and routine, non-instructive communications as with inducement, specific intent cannot be plausibly inferred without concrete allegations of targeted promotion or instruction for the carved-out method. Justice Kagan’s middle-ground approach also fits my pragmatic concerns: a skinny label is not an absolute shield, but at the pleading stage it is strongly probative against intent absent facts showing affirmative steps directed to prescribers/pharmacists to bring about the patented use. Treating generic entry plus foreseeable downstream prescribing as “inducement” would, in practice, convert Congress’s carve-out into a litigation trap that delays access and raises costs borne most heavily by vulnerable patients—an outcome I cannot square with the statute’s structure or our inducement precedents.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains that, in Hatch-Waxman, a generic can predict—and economically benefit from—substitution into the patented use even with a skinny label, so intent should be inferable from launching an AB-rated product. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Twombly/Iqbal requires allegations that make specific intent plausible rather than merely conceivable, and conduct equally consistent with Congress’s § viii carve-out (FDA-compliant labeling plus ordinary sales) cannot by itself support the Global-Tech/Grokster requirement of purposeful encouragement. Justice Gorsuch’s emphasis on the statutory adverb “actively” is textually salient: if foreseeability plus market structure sufficed, “actively induces” would collapse into “sells knowing some infringement will occur,” effectively nullifying the carve-out’s practical utility. I therefore stick with the middle-ground rule: a skinny label is not an absolute shield, but plaintiffs must plead concrete, targeted acts encouraging the patented method beyond “market realities,” which is not done here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains that, given AB-rating and automatic substitution, launching a generic makes patented-use infringement highly predictable, so intent should be inferable notwithstanding a skinny label. But as the Chief Justice stresses, Twombly/Iqbal requires allegations that plausibly distinguish unlawful, purpose-driven encouragement from conduct “at least equally consistent” with Congress’s lawful § viii carve-out pathway; market predictability alone does not do that. Global-Tech and Grokster make “purposeful, culpable” affirmative steps the hinge, and reading “actively induces” to cover mere participation in a regulated market would collapse specific intent into foreseeability and drain “actively” of independent work. Justice Kagan’s point that a skinny label is not categorically dispositive is correct, yet it reinforces—not weakens—the need for concrete, targeted encouraging acts tied to the patented indication, which the pleadings as described lack.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Respondent’s best theory—that in Hatch-Waxman the generic’s knowledge of AB-rating, state substitution, and prescribing patterns makes infringement so predictable that intent can be inferred—still collapses § 271(b)’s “actively induces” into mere foreseeability. Chief Justice Roberts’s Twombly/Iqbal framing is decisive for me: where the pleaded conduct is at least as consistent with lawful § viii carve-out compliance and routine, non-instructive communications as with purposeful encouragement, the complaint does not plausibly allege the specific intent Global-Tech and Grokster require. Justice Kagan’s middle-ground point (skinny labels are not categorically dispositive) is correct as a matter of doctrine, but it only underscores the pleading deficiency here absent concrete allegations of targeted promotion or instruction of the patented method. Institutionally and practically, treating predictable downstream substitution as inducement would destabilize the carve-out regime Congress designed by converting lawful participation in that pathway into a liability trigger.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains that, in light of substitution laws and AB-rating, the generic could foresee (and even economically benefit from) some patented-use prescriptions notwithstanding a skinny label. But as Justice Gorsuch stresses, § 271(b)’s text—“actively induces”—demands affirmative, purposeful steps to bring about the infringing method, and Global-Tech/Grokster require plausibly alleged culpable intent, not an inference drawn from predictable market mechanics. Chief Justice Roberts’s Twombly/Iqbal framing is decisive for me: where the pleaded facts are at least equally consistent with Congress’s authorized § viii carve-out and FDA-compliant labeling as with targeted encouragement of the carved-out use, the complaint does not cross the plausibility threshold. I therefore would hold only that these allegations of “market realities” and generalized, non-instructive statements are insufficient at the 12(b)(6) stage, without adopting a categorical rule that skinny labels always defeat inducement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that a generic can “intend” the patented use because it knows AB-rating and state substitution laws will predictably channel prescriptions into infringing administration, but that theory—standing alone—collapses § 271(b)’s specific-intent requirement into mere foreseeability and would threaten Congress’s § viii carve-out as a practical matter. I agree with Justice Kagan’s framing that a skinny label is not categorically dispositive, yet under Twombly/Iqbal the complaint still must allege objective, targeted acts of encouragement tied to the patented method (e.g., prescriber/pharmacist-directed instructions), not investor-facing or generalized market statements equally consistent with lawful conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, Global-Tech and Grokster demand purposeful, culpable conduct—“actively induc[ing]”—so “market realities” without more do not plausibly plead inducement at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Nothing in colleagues’ cited precedents undercuts that the pleadings here leave a lawful explanation at least as plausible as an unlawful one, so dismissal remains warranted.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires purposeful encouragement of infringement, not mere foreseeability that substitution laws and market dynamics will lead to some infringing use. Under Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and Grokster, inducement turns on specific intent shown through affirmative, culpable conduct; when the generic has filed a lawful § viii carve-out “skinny label,” allegations resting primarily on FDA-mandated labeling status, therapeutic equivalence, and generalized public statements must, under Twombly/Iqbal, plausibly support an inference of intent beyond lawful explanations. Allowing such allegations to survive routinely at Rule 12(b)(6) would risk converting Congress’s carve-out pathway into a de facto trap for generic entry, undermining the Hatch-Waxman framework and institutional predictability. The proper course is to require more particularized factual allegations of targeted promotion of the patented method before imposing discovery and potential liability under § 271(b).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces” infringement, which, under the statute’s text and this Court’s precedents, requires purposeful, culpable conduct and specific intent—not mere knowledge or foreseeability that infringement may occur in the market. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. makes clear that inducement demands proof of intent to bring about the infringing acts, and Twombly/Iqbal requires complaint allegations that plausibly support that intent rather than speculation premised on lawful conduct consistent with Congress’s Hatch-Waxman carve-out pathway. Where the generic’s FDA-approved label omits the patented indication, allegations resting primarily on “market realities” (e.g., substitution laws and therapeutic equivalence) and non-instructive, lawful communications do not plausibly plead the requisite affirmative “active steps” to encourage the patented method, because such theories collapse intent into foreseeability contrary to § 271(b)’s original meaning. Accordingly, the inducement claim should not proceed past Rule 12(b)(6) on these pleadings.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who "actively induces" infringement, which this Court has understood to require purposeful, culpable conduct and specific intent—not mere foreseeability that infringement may occur in the marketplace. See Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754, 766 (2011); MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd., 545 U.S. 913, 937 (2005). At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Twombly/Iqbal requires a plausible inference of that intent; where the generic used a congressionally authorized skinny label carving out the patented indication, the alleged "other communications" that are equally consistent with lawful commercial behavior do not plausibly rule in an intent to cause the patented use. Allowing such allegations to proceed would effectively convert lawful Hatch-Waxman Section viii conduct into a de facto basis for inducement, undermining the statutory pathway for generic entry and inviting speculative litigation untethered from affirmative encouragement of the patented method.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only for purposeful encouragement of infringement, not for mere foreseeability that some infringing use will occur in a regulated market; Global-Tech requires knowledge and specific intent, and Grokster likewise demands “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct.” At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Twombly/Iqbal require plausible factual allegations that make an inference of intent to induce the patented method more likely than lawful explanations—here, compliance with Hatch-Waxman’s § viii skinny-label pathway and FDA-driven communications. Allowing inducement to proceed on allegations grounded chiefly in substitution laws, market “realities,” or generic investor/market statements risks converting Congress’s authorized carve-out mechanism into a trap that chills generic entry and raises drug costs for patients who rely on affordable medicines. The better course is to treat a properly carved-out label as strongly probative against intent absent well-pleaded, concrete allegations of affirmative promotion of the patented use directed to prescribers or dispensers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces infringement,” which under Global-Tech requires knowledge of the patent and a specific intent to bring about the infringing acts—not merely awareness that infringement may occur as a foreseeable byproduct of lawful sales in a regulated market. At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Twombly/Iqbal require allegations that make inducement more than a lawful “skinny label” plus market substitution realities and investor-facing “puffery”; the complaint must plausibly allege affirmative, purposeful encouragement of the patented method, not just communications consistent with noninfringing uses. Treating non-label statements and background substitution practices as enough to infer intent would, as a practical matter, swallow Hatch-Waxman’s section viii carve-out mechanism by making generic entry contingent on disproving downstream prescribing behavior. A workable middle ground is to recognize that a skinny label is not categorically dispositive, but to require plausibly pleaded, concrete inducement acts tied to the patented use—something not adequately alleged here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces” infringement, and that text—especially the adverb “actively”—demands affirmative steps undertaken with the purpose of bringing about the infringing use, not mere awareness that infringement may foreseeably occur in a regulated marketplace. Global-Tech makes clear that inducement turns on knowledge and specific intent, and Twombly/Iqbal require a complaint to plead facts that plausibly support that culpable intent rather than leaving an equally obvious lawful explanation (such as FDA-authorized “section viii” carve-outs and investor-directed or otherwise non-instructive communications) standing unrebutted at the motion-to-dismiss stage. On the allegations described here—where the generic label excludes the patented indication and the remaining theory relies heavily on market realities like substitution practices and ambiguous public statements—the complaint risks collapsing specific intent into foreseeability, contradicting the statute’s plain meaning and this Court’s inducement cases (including Grokster’s focus on purposeful promotion). I would reverse and require more particularized, non-conclusory allegations of affirmative encouragement of the patented method to proceed past Rule 12(b)(6).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires purposeful encouragement and specific intent to cause infringement, not merely foreseeability that some infringing uses will occur in the Hatch-Waxman marketplace. Under Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and Grokster, inducement turns on affirmative, culpable conduct directed to the patented method, and Twombly/Iqbal require allegations that plausibly support that unlawful intent rather than lawful explanations—especially where Congress affirmatively authorized a Section viii “skinny label” pathway that carves out the patented indication. Allowing an inducement claim to proceed based largely on generic market realities (substitution laws, therapeutic equivalence) and non-instructive communications risks converting method-of-use patents into de facto barriers contrary to the practical workability of the Hatch-Waxman framework. On these allegations at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, the complaint does not plausibly plead the requisite specific intent and active inducement beyond lawful skinny-label compliance.

Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. confirms that inducement demands a heightened mens rea (knowledge/intent, including willful blindness) and, coupled with Grokster’s insistence on “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct,” counsels against treating ordinary, facially lawful acts incident to FDA-regulated product distribution (including a compliant skinny label and non-instructive communications) as sufficient. At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Twombly/Iqbal require allegations that plausibly support specific intent to encourage the patented method and plausibly rule out lawful explanations such as investor-oriented puffery or the predictable effects of state substitution laws and therapeutic equivalence rules. Because the pleaded “market realities” and generalized communications do not plausibly amount to affirmative encouragement or instruction of the patented indication beyond what the label disclaims, the complaint fails to state a claim for inducement under § 271(b).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, § 271(b) still requires a plausible inference of purposeful encouragement and specific intent to bring about the patented method, not merely knowledge that substitution laws and market realities will predictably result in some infringing use. Under Twombly/Iqbal, where the pleaded communications are equally (or more) consistent with lawful, FDA-authorized Section viii “skinny label” conduct and routine commercial or investor statements, the complaint must allege objective, particularized facts that plausibly tip the inference toward intent to induce infringement rather than lawful explanations. Global-Tech confirms that inducement turns on a culpable mental state—knowledge/intent—and allowing a claim to proceed on generic, non-instructive communications risks converting compliance with Hatch-Waxman’s carve-out pathway into de facto liability, with significant practical consequences for access and cost. Because the allegations here (as framed) do not plausibly “nudge” intent beyond lawful conduct into § 271(b) inducement, I would reverse and require more specific, targeted inducing acts tied to the patented use.
